header: 2Seven Decades of Video Games along Three Axes

images.caption: Figure 1:Seven decades of games along graphics, interaction, and gameplay.Eras are delimited by transitions in graphics, and each dated landmark is placed in the era of its release. Interaction is split as in Section1: coarse-grained interaction moves the camera and the protagonist; fine-grained interaction is what the protagonist does to objects and characters.

Figure 2:GameWM maximizes generative capability subject to game stability.Designs run from traditional CG (left) to pure world models (right). Each is a stack of the four modules of a frame, with world state at the bottom: purple blocks are produced by a neural network, grey blocks by the engine, and the label above each gap names the module the network takes over between two neighboring designs. The curves are schematic, not measured.

Figure 3:From authored assets to play.Left: authored once, a first frame and a character sheet, and a skill tree that fuses an attribute of the sheet (fire) with each mechanic. Middle: at run time the GameWM-engine renders low-poly proxy frames and resolves the event, here a ranged attack that becomes Fireball. Right: the four inputs fill the slots of the GameWM-VM’s reference interface (H3’s Ref2VA, Section6); the output column shows frames of a BD-Sheet sample generated from them.

Figure 4:The interaction-centric data engine.Left: both source paths yield the same three proxies and an event caption, from which H3 Ref2VA rendersmmlow-poly andnnhigh-fidelity versions of the clip. After VLM screening, each of the three proxies and themmlow-poly videos is paired with every high-fidelity target and with the source recording. Right: one “enter vehicle” clip withm=n=4m=n=4, giving7×4=287\times 4=28stylized pairs, plus seven with the recording (not drawn); the outlined cell is the pair shown above the grid.

Figure 5:Composition of the data engine by source clips.Left: the share of each source. Right: the event of every clip, with granularity on the inner ring and the event on the outer ring; hue gives the source, and height the granularity (fine-grained, coarse, untagged). ABot-World is the released 500-hour, action-annotated part of the training data of ABot-World-0[ABot-World Team, 2026], with depth and semantics estimated by MoGe-3[Kong et al., 2026]and SAM 2[Ravi et al., 2025]; CARLA[Dosovitskiy et al., 2017]and Magpie[Zhan and others, 2026]come from SolarRenderer-Data[Fang et al., 2026]. Shares are of the snapshot in Table6.

Figure 6:One training pair per engine event.Each block shows a clip’s capsule re-render, which is the proxy, above the source recording. The first two rows are fine-grained GTA V events; the rest are coarse or untagged clips from GTA V, Magpie, ABot-World, and CARLA. Red ticks mark engine state changes. The capsules carry the camera, the layout, and the timing of each event, but no limbs, faces, or effects.

Figure 7:Every proxy on one held-out vehicle entry.Top: the recorded game. Below, each group shows a proxy above the bidirectional output it drives: three engine buffers (DUV, depth, semantic), three coarse re-renders (low-poly, voxel, capsule), and a static control in which the first DUV frame is held for the whole clip. Red ticks mark the engine’s entry start and seated frames.

Figure 8:One mechanic, many realizations: ranged and melee.The left four columns are the shooting clip and the right four a melee clip; each clip keeps one capsule proxy and one caption template (the box above its columns). Each row is one character: its sheet and name (far left), a first frame of that character in each scene, and its skill for each mechanic (the tag on the first frame of each clip). BD-Sheet, 30 steps; red ticks mark the shot, the strike, and the fall as read off the proxies. The DMD-Sheet version of the ranged clip is in Figure13.

Figure 9:One character across scenes.Four characters (left, with their sheets), each in four scenes: three shooting clips and a held-out vehicle entry, all driven by capsule proxies. Each first frame is authored for its scene from the sheet. BD-Sheet model; columns from 0 to 5 s. The DMD-Sheet version is in Figure14.

Figure 10:Bidirectional teacher and causal student on four events.Each group shows the proxy above the bidirectional output (30 steps, whole clip) and the DMD output (4 steps per chunk). Shoot: the shooting clip with its capsule proxy; Enter, Exit, Melee: held-out clips under semantic, DUV, and capsule proxies. Columns are chosen per event; red ticks mark the engine’s event frames (for the two attacks, read off the proxy).

Figure 11:Four-step causal students across backbones.The same capsule proxy (top), fire-mage sheet, first frame, and caption for every model; for each model, the three of eight seeds that follow the proxy most closely. GameWM-H3-33B is DMD-Sheet; the Wan2.2 students are distilled from their sheet-conditioned bidirectional models. Columns are times on the 24 fps clip (the 14B student renders 16 fps); red ticks mark the shot and the fall in the proxy.

Figure 12:Characters and their skills, causal model.One capsule proxy and one caption template (top); each row adds a character sheet (left), a first frame of that character, and the character’s skill (row label). DMD-Sheet, 4 steps per chunk; one frame from the middle of each chunk, dashed lines at chunk boundaries.
Figure 14:One character across scenes, causal model.The scenes, sheets, first frames, and captions of Figure9, rendered by DMD-Sheet at 4 steps per chunk; columns from 0 to 5 s.
